narrative:
The decision to deny your application rests on a prediction that you have a 52.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. While this is not an overwhelming majority, it means that the model sees you as slightly more likely to fail than to pass, and for a high-stakes professional outcome, that level of risk was enough to tip the decision against you.

The single strongest factor pushing toward failure was your academic standing in your third year. You placed in the second decile of your class, while students who were accepted typically sit around the sixth decile. This wide gap strongly suggested that your performance in advanced law coursework was not tracking toward bar readiness. Your first-year standing also worked against you, though somewhat less strongly. Ranking in the third decile, again against an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, showed a pattern of academic struggle that compounded the concern from your later years.

One factor did work in your favor. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.30 sits above the accepted-student average of 3.23, and this pushed the prediction toward passing. However, this positive influence was not strong enough to overcome the two negative signals from your law school class rank.

Moving forward, your clearest path is to focus on raising your class standing, particularly in your upper-level courses. Because your law school grades are what most strongly drive the predicted risk of bar failure, demonstrating a sustained upward trend in your academic performance would directly address the model's main concern and give a future reviewer more reason to believe you can pass.
